title: The Hidden Passage — routes, adjacency, and work that survives
question: In a declared finite four-coordinate routing world, how do obstacle placement, access, adjacency, observation and retained search affect exact routes and repeated work?
method: Closed-form route bounds, independent finite shortest-path oracles, shortest-path DAG mask propagation, and resumable reverse Dijkstra, with full world-signature keys.
finding: For the defined wall D(d,c)=8+min(8,2c(d+1)) for d<=2; D(3,c)=16. The recorded checks cover 16 wall-cost pairs, 96 smaller-world route questions and 560 streamed route answers. Retained reverse search cuts declared work events sharply on repeated-destination workloads but increases them slightly for one-off destinations.
claim_scope: Finite simulated weighted graphs with known geometry and unit work-event accounting. Exact statements are about the specified model, not physical four-dimensional space or traffic engineering.
limitations: W is a spatial coordinate of a stipulated mathematical model, not time or observed physics.
Access-cost and adjacency signals are stipulated; no queue capacity, energy, collision, or construction costs.
Work events are declared counters, not seconds, energy or real traffic delay.
Reuse fails on one-off destination queries and is unsound if the world signature is dropped after an edit.
open_questions: Can a genuine, measured information-transfer benefit be connected to the proposed adjacency model?
When does retaining and indexing existing route work outperform other demand-driven caches under measured machine costs?
